topic: Figma integrates AI agents and code layers
headline_marked: [[Figma launches new AI agent features]] & Markdown editor for design systems at India event
headline: Figma launches new AI agent features & Markdown editor for design systems at India event
summary: Figma introduces 'Specs' for Markdown-based design language definition and opens Code Layers to public beta, enhancing AI agent adherence to brand guidelines and enabling interactive prototypes.
details: Figma unveiled new features at its first Config event in India, including a Markdown-based editor called Figma Specs and public beta for Code Layers. These tools aim to help define design systems and integrate with AI agents for more consistent brand adherence.

Figma Specs allows users to define design language simply, serving as a reference for teams and AI agents. It can exist as a standalone file or within the canvas, embedding FigJam diagrams, code layers, and designs.

The platform now provides more context for design, including libraries and guidelines, to manage design systems. This centralized system helps agents adhere to specific rules, steering AI towards more predictable outcomes.
The Code Layers feature, which adds coding to designs for interactive prototypes, is now in public beta. Users can ask agents to turn designs into code or modify existing code for rapid prototyping.

Figma is also supporting over 20 new tools with its MCP, including Open Code and Indian AI startup Sarvam. Additionally, it integrated its acquired headless CMS, Payload, with Figma Make for dynamic website generation and content management.

Figma's chief design officer noted that AI enables more code production for product discovery, not just shipping. India is Figma's largest market outside the US, with the company working with 40% of India's top 100 Bombay Stock Exchange companies.

topic: Apple HomeView screen requires iPhone for setup
headline_marked: [[Apple's $299 HomeView screen requires an iPhone]] for setup, making it useless for Android users
headline: Apple's $299 HomeView screen requires an iPhone for setup, making it useless for Android users
summary: Apple's new HomeView screen, priced at $299, cannot be set up without a compatible iPhone or iPad. This crucial requirement is not prominently displayed on the main product page.
details: Apple's new HomeView screen, costing $299, cannot be set up on its own. Official footnotes state that a compatible iPhone or iPad running the latest software is required for initial setup. Without an Apple device, the screen remains a non-functional display.

The main HomeView product page does not feature a prominent system requirements section. This key detail is often buried in small notes or FAQs, leading many buyers to discover the necessity of an iPhone only after purchase.

The requirement goes beyond initial setup; the screen integrates with Apple's Home app for a full, personalized experience. This means the "home" environment lives within the Apple ecosystem, effectively locking out Android users from core functionalities.

While the product page mentions that guests can use some screen features without full integration, the fundamental setup process still mandates an Apple device. This design choice appears to be a form of ecosystem lock-in, though it may also simplify password entry.

Potential buyers are advised to check the "System Requirements" section on the specs page before purchasing, especially when buying as a gift. The article highlights the importance of understanding device compatibility to avoid disappointment.
